issues.title: The stated boundary condition controls the wrong component

failure_location.quote: Our assumption is the minimal requirement to satisfy Stokes theorem in the proof of the main result as well as for numerical simulation purposes.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: divergence-free smooth vector fields taking values on $\Omega$ which are parallel to the boundary

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the preceding assumption—vanishing tangential velocity—is the minimal boundary requirement needed for the proof and simulations. The old proof actually produces the boundary term involving k δv·n, so it is the normal component that must vanish; the coordinate-system discussion likewise identifies admissible vector fields as parallel to the boundary. The later condition v=0 is sufficient and salvages the formal proof, but it is stronger than necessary and does not make the earlier component description or minimality claim correct.
issues.overall_effect: The paper misstates the geometric boundary contract and its proof rationale, although the later no-slip condition is strong enough that the old formal results remain established on their narrower admissible class.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace “the tangential component of v vanishes” with the impermeability condition v·n=0, equivalently that v is tangent to the boundary. Restrict the minimality rationale to cancellation of the Stokes boundary term and retain the later condition v=0 as a stronger assumption.
issues.why_classification: The boundary integral k δv·n and the old source's description of admissible fields as parallel to the boundary uniquely force normal, rather than tangential, vanishing. A knowledgeable reader can make that transcriptional component correction without repairing any inference, and the formal results already use the sufficient no-slip condition.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Throughout the paper, we assume that $\Omega$ is a bounded domain and that the velocity field is tangent to the boundary.

issues.title: Reciprocal obstacle potential contradicts the stated smooth variational class

failure_location.quote:
The potential function $V$ is an artificial smooth (or at least $C^{2}$) potential function
associated with a fictitious force inducing a repulsion from a region $S\subset\Omega$.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: To avoid collision with obstacles we introduce a potential function $V$ defined as the inverse value of the function $f$.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that V is a smooth, or at least C2, potential usable in the full-domain variational problem. The paper actually defines the obstacle surface inside Ω by a zero of f and proposes V=1/f, specifically with denominator (x-a)^2+(y-b)^2+(z-c)^2-r^2. That denominator vanishes on the obstacle surface; near a regular zero set the reciprocal behaves like the inverse normal distance and is not even locally integrable, while its gradient is still more singular. Thus the proposed V is neither C2 on Ω nor a well-defined input to the displayed full-domain functional and first variation.
issues.overall_effect: The reciprocal obstacle example cannot instantiate the stated functional or its gradient-based extremal calculation. The generic derivation for genuinely regular potentials is not thereby defeated.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the reciprocal profile V=1/f with a genuinely regular obstacle-shaping potential satisfying the functional's integrability and differentiability requirements. Remove the blow-up and guaranteed-nonintersection assertions, describe the surviving mechanism as soft obstacle penalization, and retain the generic variational derivation for regular V.
issues.why_classification: A reciprocal across a regular zero hypersurface cannot be made admissible by a local regularity qualification; retaining a singular hard barrier would require reformulating the domain, functional, and first variation. A contained smooth replacement preserves a recognizably comparable obstacle-penalization framework, but meaningfully weakens guaranteed avoidance to soft penalization, so the issue exceeds minor without requiring global reconstruction.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: where $V:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ is a $C^1$ function in the Sobolev space $H^{1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d})$.

issues.title: The claimed repulsive potential contributes an inward source

failure_location.quote:
The potential function $V$ is an artificial smooth (or at least $C^{2}$) potential function
associated with a fictitious force inducing a repulsion from a region $S\subset\Omega$.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the chosen potential induces repulsion from the obstacle. What the old paper actually specifies is the source +∇V together with V=1/(ρ²-r²). In the admissible exterior regime ρ>r, ∇V=-2q/(ρ²-r²)², where q is the outward radial displacement, so the source points toward the obstacle center. The material difference is a complete reversal of the asserted force direction, not merely a change in magnitude.
issues.overall_effect: The old reciprocal profile cannot support the paper's repulsive-force interpretation or the corresponding obstacle-avoidance interpretation of the numerical illustration, although this does not by itself invalidate the displayed generic modified Euler equation.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: With the displayed source term +∇V retained, reverse the sign of the selected exterior radial profile, or replace it by an equivalent profile whose gradient points outward, and rerun and relabel the affected numerical illustration.
issues.why_classification: The force-direction defect is repaired by an elementary, local sign or profile correction. The generic modified Euler equation, derivation, numerical method, and intended outward-shaping claim can otherwise remain unchanged; regenerating the numerical output is routine. It is not a typo because the old computation actually used the inward-pointing profile and more than one sign convention could have been changed.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Since the reduced modified Euler equation \eqref{mod:eulereq} contains the term \(+\nabla V\), this choice yields an outward shaping term in the neighborhood of the obstacle.

issues.title: A final-only projection does not enforce incompressibility during evolution

failure_location.quote: Therefore, after the time integration stage is completed we projected our solution to a divergence free-vector field using the approach explained in the previous section.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The result of discretizing the first equation in \eqref{mod:eulereq} using a finite difference scheme may result in a discrete vector field with discrete divergence, even though we depart from divergence-free initial conditions.

issues.failure_explanation: The procedure is presented as an integration of the modified incompressible Euler equations, whose velocity must remain divergence-free. The old text acknowledges that the finite-difference update can create discrete divergence, yet projects only after all 140 updates. Thus the intermediate inputs to subsequent convective updates violate the algorithm's incompressibility contract; projecting the final output fixes only that output, not the trajectory that generated it.
issues.overall_effect: The final field may be projected to zero discrete divergence, but the reported evolution and resulting simulation are not established as an approximation that enforces the incompressible constraint throughout time. The numerical results must be recomputed with the corrected loop.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: After every finite-difference update X*, solve Δdφ=∇d·X*, set X^(n+1)=X*−∇dφ, and use that projected field in the next convective update. Rerun the complete evolution and replace all trajectory-dependent figures and numerical statements.
issues.why_classification: The paper already defines the required discrete Helmholtz projection, so placing that existing operation inside the time-stepping loop is a standard, local, source-supported correction that restores discrete incompressibility at the states propagated forward. Although the old trajectory must be recomputed, no new numerical architecture, lemma, rate, or substantive weakening is required.
